Base directory for this skill: /Users/eric/.claude/plugins/cache/claude-plugins-official/superpowers/6.1.1/skills/subagent-driven-development

# Subagent-Driven Development

Execute plan by dispatching a fresh implementer subagent per task, a task review (spec compliance + code quality) after each, and a broad whole-branch review at the end.

**Why subagents:** You delegate tasks to specialized agents with isolated context. By precisely crafting their instructions and context, you ensure they stay focused and succeed at their task. They should never inherit your session's context or history — you construct exactly what they need. This also preserves your own context for coordination work.

**Core principle:** Fresh subagent per task + task review (spec + quality) + broad final review = high quality, fast iteration

**Narration:** between tool calls, narrate at most one short line — the
ledger and the tool results carry the record.

**Continuous execution:** Do not pause to check in with your human partner between tasks. Execute all tasks from the plan without stopping. The only reasons to stop are: BLOCKED status you cannot resolve, ambiguity that genuinely prevents progress, or all tasks complete. "Should I continue?" prompts and progress summaries waste their time — they asked you to execute the plan, so execute it.

## When to Use

```dot
digraph when_to_use {
    "Have implementation plan?" [shape=diamond];
    "Tasks mostly independent?" [shape=diamond];
    "Stay in this session?" [shape=diamond];
    "subagent-driven-development" [shape=box];
    "executing-plans" [shape=box];
    "Manual execution or brainstorm first" [shape=box];

    "Have implementation plan?" -> "Tasks mostly independent?" [label="yes"];
    "Have implementation plan?" -> "Manual execution or brainstorm first" [label="no"];
    "Tasks mostly independent?" -> "Stay in this session?" [label="yes"];
    "Tasks mostly independent?" -> "Manual execution or brainstorm first" [label="no - tightly coupled"];
    "Stay in this session?" -> "subagent-driven-development" [label="yes"];
    "Stay in this session?" -> "executing-plans" [label="no - parallel session"];
}
```

**vs. Executing Plans (parallel session):**
- Same session (no context switch)
- Fresh subagent per task (no context pollution)
- Review after each task (spec compliance + code quality), broad review at the end
- Faster iteration (no human-in-loop between tasks)

## The Process

```dot
digraph process {
    rankdir=TB;

    subgraph cluster_per_task {
        label="Per Task";
        "Dispatch implementer subagent (./implementer-prompt.md)" [shape=box];
        "Implementer subagent asks questions?" [shape=diamond];
        "Answer questions, provide context" [shape=box];
        "Implementer subagent implements, tests, commits, self-reviews" [shape=box];
        "Write diff file, dispatch task reviewer subagent (./task-reviewer-prompt.md)" [shape=box];
        "Task reviewer reports spec ✅ and quality approved?" [shape=diamond];
        "Dispatch fix subagent for Critical/Important findings" [shape=box];
        "Mark task complete in todo list and progress ledger" [shape=box];
    }

    "Read plan, note context and global constraints, create todos" [shape=box];
    "More tasks remain?" [shape=diamond];
    "Dispatch final code reviewer subagent (../requesting-code-review/code-reviewer.md)" [shape=box];
    "Use superpowers:finishing-a-development-branch" [shape=box style=filled fillcolor=lightgreen];

    "Read plan, note context and global constraints, create todos" -> "Dispatch implementer subagent (./implementer-prompt.md)";
    "Dispatch implementer subagent (./implementer-prompt.md)" -> "Implementer subagent asks questions?";
    "Implementer subagent asks questions?" -> "Answer questions, provide context" [label="yes"];
    "Answer questions, provide context" -> "Dispatch implementer subagent (./implementer-prompt.md)";
    "Implementer subagent asks questions?" -> "Implementer subagent implements, tests, commits, self-reviews" [label="no"];
    "Implementer subagent implements, tests, commits, self-reviews" -> "Write diff file, dispatch task reviewer subagent (./task-reviewer-prompt.md)";
    "Write diff file, dispatch task reviewer subagent (./task-reviewer-prompt.md)" -> "Task reviewer reports spec ✅ and quality approved?";
    "Task reviewer reports spec ✅ and quality approved?" -> "Dispatch fix subagent for Critical/Important findings" [label="no"];
    "Dispatch fix subagent for Critical/Important findings" -> "Write diff file, dispatch task reviewer subagent (./task-reviewer-prompt.md)" [label="re-review"];
    "Task reviewer reports spec ✅ and quality approved?" -> "Mark task complete in todo list and progress ledger" [label="yes"];
    "Mark task complete in todo list and progress ledger" -> "More tasks remain?";
    "More tasks remain?" -> "Dispatch implementer subagent (./implementer-prompt.md)" [label="yes"];
    "More tasks remain?" -> "Dispatch final code reviewer subagent (../requesting-code-review/code-reviewer.md)" [label="no"];
    "Dispatch final code reviewer subagent (../requesting-code-review/code-reviewer.md)" -> "Use superpowers:finishing-a-development-branch";
}
```

## Pre-Flight Plan Review

Before dispatching Task 1, scan the plan once for conflicts:

- tasks that contradict each other or the plan's Global Constraints
- anything the plan explicitly mandates that the review rubric treats as a
  defect (a test that asserts nothing, verbatim duplication of a logic block)

Present everything you find to your human partner as one batched question —
each finding beside the plan text that mandates it, asking which governs —
before execution begins, not one interrupt per discovery mid-plan. If the
scan is clean, proceed without comment. The review loop remains the net for
conflicts that only emerge from implementation.

## Model Selection

Use the least powerful model that can handle each role to conserve cost and increase speed.

**Mechanical implementation tasks** (isolated functions, clear specs, 1-2 files): use a fast, cheap model. Most implementation tasks are mechanical when the plan is well-specified.

**Integration and judgment tasks** (multi-file coordination, pattern matching, debugging): use a standard model.

**Architecture and design tasks**: use the most capable available model.
The final whole-branch review is one of these — dispatch it on the most
capable available model, not the session default.

**Review tasks**: choose the model with the same judgment, scaled to the
diff's size, complexity, and risk. A small mechanical diff does not need the
most capable model; a subtle concurrency change does.

**Always specify the model explicitly when dispatching a subagent.** An
omitted model inherits your session's model — often the most capable and
most expensive — which silently defeats this section.

**Turn count beats token price.** Wall-clock and context cost scale with how
many turns a subagent takes, and the cheapest models routinely take 2-3× the
turns on multi-step work — costing more overall. Use a mid-tier model as the
floor for reviewers and for implementers working from prose descriptions.
When the task's plan text contains the complete code to write, the
implementation is transcription plus testing: use the cheapest tier for
that implementer. Single-file mechanical fixes also take the cheapest tier.

**Task complexity signals (implementation tasks):**
- Touches 1-2 files with a complete spec → cheap model
- Touches multiple files with integration concerns → standard model
- Requires design judgment or broad codebase understanding → most capable model

## Handling Implementer Status

Implementer subagents report one of four statuses. Handle each appropriately:

**DONE:** Generate the review package (`scripts/review-package BASE HEAD`, from this skill's directory — it prints the unique file path it wrote; BASE is the commit you recorded before dispatching the implementer — never `HEAD~1`, which silently drops all but the last commit of a multi-commit task), then dispatch the task reviewer with the printed path.

**DONE_WITH_CONCERNS:** The implementer completed the work but flagged doubts. Read the concerns before proceeding. If the concerns are about correctness or scope, address them before review. If they're observations (e.g., "this file is getting large"), note them and proceed to review.

**NEEDS_CONTEXT:** The implementer needs information that wasn't provided. Provide the missing context and re-dispatch.

**BLOCKED:** The implementer cannot complete the task. Assess the blocker:
1. If it's a context problem, provide more context and re-dispatch with the same model
2. If the task requires more reasoning, re-dispatch with a more capable model
3. If the task is too large, break it into smaller pieces
4. If the plan itself is wrong, escalate to the human

**Never** ignore an escalation or force the same model to retry without changes. If the implementer said it's stuck, something needs to change.

## Handling Reviewer ⚠️ Items

The task reviewer may report "⚠️ Cannot verify from diff" items — requirements
that live in unchanged code or span tasks. These do not block the rest of the
review, but you must resolve each one yourself before marking the task
complete: you hold the plan and cross-task context the reviewer
lacks. If you confirm an item is a real gap, treat it as a failed spec
review — send it back to the implementer and re-review.

## Constructing Reviewer Prompts

Per-task reviews are task-scoped gates. The broad review happens once, at the
final whole-branch review. When you fill a reviewer template:

- Do not add open-ended directives like "check all uses" or "run race tests
  if useful" without a concrete, task-specific reason
- Do not ask a reviewer to re-run tests the implementer already ran on the
  same code — the implementer's report carries the test evidence
- Do not pre-judge findings for the reviewer — never instruct a reviewer to
  ignore or not flag a specific issue. If you believe a finding would be a
  false positive, let the reviewer raise it and adjudicate it in the review
  loop. If the prompt you are writing contains "do not flag," "don't treat X
  as a defect," "at most Minor," or "the plan chose" — stop: you are
  pre-judging, usually to spare yourself a review loop.
- The global-constraints block you hand the reviewer is its attention
  lens. Copy the binding requirements verbatim from the plan's Global
  Constraints section or the spec: exact values, exact formats, and the
  stated relationships between components ("same layout as X", "matches
  Y"). The reviewer's template already carries the process rules (YAGNI,
  test hygiene, review method) — the constraints block is for what THIS
  project's spec demands.
- Hand the reviewer its diff as a file: run this skill's
  `scripts/review-package BASE HEAD` and pass the reviewer the file path
  it prints (or, without bash: `git log --oneline`, `git diff --stat`,
  and `git diff -U10` for the range, redirected to one uniquely named
  file). The output never enters your own context, and the reviewer sees
  the commit list, stat summary, and full diff with context in one Read
  call. Use the BASE you recorded before dispatching the implementer —
  never `HEAD~1`, which silently truncates multi-commit tasks.
- A dispatch prompt describes one task, not the session's history. Do not
  paste accumulated prior-task summaries ("state after Tasks 1-3") into
  later dispatches — a real session's dispatch hit 42k chars of which 99%
  was pasted history. A fresh subagent needs its task, the interfaces it
  touches, and the global constraints. Nothing else.
- Dispatch fix subagents for Critical and Important findings. Record Minor
  findings in the progress ledger as you go, and point the final
  whole-branch review at that list so it can triage which must be fixed
  before merge. A roll-up nobody reads is a silent discard.
- A finding labeled plan-mandated — or any finding that conflicts with
  what the plan's text requires — is the human's decision, like any plan
  contradiction: present the finding and the plan text, ask which governs.
  Do not dismiss the finding because the plan mandates it, and do not
  dispatch a fix that contradicts the plan without asking.
- The final whole-branch review gets a package too: run
  `scripts/review-package MERGE_BASE HEAD` (MERGE_BASE = the commit the
  branch started from, e.g. `git merge-base main HEAD`) and include the
  printed path in the final review dispatch, so the final reviewer reads
  one file instead of re-deriving the branch diff with git commands.
- Every fix dispatch carries the implementer contract: the fix subagent
  re-runs the tests covering its change and reports the results. Name the
  covering test files in the dispatch — a one-line fix does not need the
  whole suite. Before re-dispatching the reviewer, confirm the fix report
  contains the covering tests, the command run, and the output; dispatch
  the re-review once all three are present.
- If the final whole-branch review returns findings, dispatch ONE fix
  subagent with the complete findings list — not one fixer per finding.
  Per-finding fixers each rebuild context and re-run suites; a real
  session's final-review fix wave cost more than all its tasks combined.

## File Handoffs

Everything you paste into a dispatch prompt — and everything a subagent
prints back — stays resident in your context for the rest of the session
and is re-read on every later turn. Hand artifacts over as files:

- **Task brief:** before dispatching an implementer, run this skill's
  `scripts/task-brief PLAN_FILE N` — it extracts the task's full text to a
  uniquely named file and prints the path. Compose the dispatch so the
  brief stays the single source of requirements. Your dispatch should
  contain: (1) one line on where this task fits in the project; (2) the
  brief path, introduced as "read this first — it is your requirements,
  with the exact values to use verbatim"; (3) interfaces and decisions
  from earlier tasks that the brief cannot know; (4) your resolution of
  any ambiguity you noticed in the brief; (5) the report-file path and
  report contract. Exact values (numbers, magic strings, signatures, test
  cases) appear only in the brief.
- **Report file:** name the implementer's report file after the brief
  (brief `…/task-N-brief.md` → report `…/task-N-report.md`) and put it in
  the dispatch prompt. The implementer writes the full report there and
  returns only status, commits, a one-line test summary, and concerns.
- **Reviewer inputs:** the task reviewer gets three paths — the same brief
  file, the report file, and the review package — plus the global
  constraints that bind the task.
- Fix dispatches append their fix report (with test results) to the same
  report file and return a short summary; re-reviews read the updated file.

## Durable Progress

Conversation memory does not survive compaction. In real sessions,
controllers that lost their place have re-dispatched entire completed task
sequences — the single most expensive failure observed. Track progress in
a ledger file, not only in todos.

- At skill start, check for a ledger:
  `cat "$(git rev-parse --show-toplevel)/.superpowers/sdd/progress.md"`. Tasks listed there
  as complete are DONE — do not re-dispatch them; resume at the first task
  not marked complete.
- When a task's review comes back clean, append one line to the ledger in
  the same message as your other bookkeeping:
  `Task N: complete (commits <base7>..<head7>, review clean)`.
- The ledger is your recovery map: the commits it names exist in git even
  when your context no longer remembers creating them. After compaction,
  trust the ledger and `git log` over your own recollection.
- `git clean -fdx` will destroy the ledger (it's git-ignored scratch); if
  that happens, recover from `git log`.

## Advantages

**vs. Manual execution:**
- Subagents follow TDD naturally
- Fresh context per task (no confusion)
- Parallel-safe (subagents don't interfere)
- Subagent can ask questions (before AND during work)

**vs. Executing Plans:**
- Same session (no handoff)
- Continuous progress (no waiting)
- Review checkpoints automatic

**Efficiency gains:**
- Controller curates exactly what context is needed; bulk artifacts move
  as files, not pasted text
- Subagent gets complete information upfront
- Questions surfaced before work begins (not after)

**Quality gates:**
- Self-review catches issues before handoff
- Task review carries two verdicts: spec compliance and code quality
- Review loops ensure fixes actually work
- Spec compliance prevents over/under-building
- Code quality ensures implementation is well-built

**Cost:**
- More subagent invocations (implementer + reviewer per task)
- Controller does more prep work (extracting all tasks upfront)
- Review loops add iterations
- But catches issues early (cheaper than debugging later)

## Red Flags

**Never:**
- Start implementation on main/master branch without explicit user consent
- Skip task review, or accept a report missing either verdict (spec compliance AND task quality are both required)
- Proceed with unfixed issues
- Dispatch multiple implementation subagents in parallel (conflicts)
- Make a subagent read the whole plan file (hand it its task brief —
  `scripts/task-brief` — instead)
- Skip scene-setting context (subagent needs to understand where task fits)
- Ignore subagent questions (answer before letting them proceed)
- Accept "close enough" on spec compliance (reviewer found spec issues = not done)
- Skip review loops (reviewer found issues = implementer fixes = review again)
- Let implementer self-review replace actual review (both are needed)
- Tell a reviewer what not to flag, or pre-rate a finding's severity in the
  dispatch prompt ("treat it as Minor at most") — the plan's example code is
  a starting point, not evidence that its weaknesses were chosen
- Dispatch a task reviewer without a diff file — generate it first
  (`scripts/review-package BASE HEAD`) and name the printed path in the
  prompt
- Move to next task while the review has open Critical/Important issues
- Re-dispatch a task the progress ledger already marks complete — check
  the ledger (and `git log`) after any compaction or resume

**If subagent asks questions:**
- Answer clearly and completely
- Provide additional context if needed
- Don't rush them into implementation

**If reviewer finds issues:**
- Implementer (same subagent) fixes them
- Reviewer reviews again
- Repeat until approved
- Don't skip the re-review

**If subagent fails task:**
- Dispatch fix subagent with specific instructions
- Don't try to fix manually (context pollution)

## Review: Task 5 — Pipeline-board UI + Era III wiring + field note

### Spec compliance: ✅

- **`lanes.ts`** — byte-for-byte match with the brief's mandated code (`LaneMeta` interface, `LANES` array for rag/wp/deps, all copy exact).
- **`index.tsx`** — byte-for-byte match with the brief's mandated code (`Era3Pipeline`, `LaneRow`, `PhaseCell`, `TICK_MS = 700`, `PHASE_COLUMN` map, tick effect).
- **`masterclass.tsx`** — imports added in sorted order (`Era3Pipeline` after `Era3Ladder`, `FieldNote` after `Era4Runtime`), era-3 children extended to `Era3Harness → Era3Ladder → Era3Pipeline → FieldNote`, exact note text (`date="2026-07"`), verified with `cat -et` that TAB indentation is preserved throughout the JSX block.
- **Interaction law** — confirmed only three interactive elements exist in the new code: `Hand off →` (rag/plan gate, only rendered while `laneState.phase === "plan"`), `Approve merge ✓` (deps/validate gate, only while `phase === "awaiting-signature"`), and `Reset`. No other `onClick` in `PhaseCell`/`LaneRow`.
- **Reduced motion** — traced the reducer: `fastForward` loops `tickBoard` while `!isSettled`, and `isSettled` treats `plan`/`awaiting-signature`/`done` as terminal, so fast-forward correctly stops at both gates rather than skipping them. Gates still require clicks under reduced motion, per spec.
- **wp `VALIDATED ✓` treatment** — matches `era3-harness/index.tsx` exactly (`bg-[#238636] text-white`, same copy).
- **Placard swap** — `done ? "Notice where your clicks went..." : "Only one column ever needs you."` matches brief text exactly, gated on `isBoardDone(state)`.
- **Deterministic** — fixed 700ms interval, no `Math.random` or non-determinism anywhere in the new files.

Nothing extra was added beyond the brief; nothing from the brief is missing.

### Tick-effect sanity check: correct, no leak

The `useEffect(..., [state])` recreates `setInterval` on every state change. Since `tickBoard`/`handOff`/`approveMerge`/`reset` all return brand-new `BoardState` objects (even when individual lane values are unchanged, e.g. ticking a lane in `plan`), every dispatch changes the `state` reference, so the effect reliably re-runs after each tick. Each interval only ever gets to fire once before its cleanup (`clearInterval`) runs on the next render, so there's no accumulation of intervals — the cleanup function always pairs with the interval it created. Once `isSettled(state)` becomes true, the effect returns early before creating a new interval, so it stops ticking cleanly (no dangling timer). This is a "restart-interval-per-render" pattern (not the most idiomatic, since it recreates a timer object every 700ms), but it is functionally correct and matches the brief's mandated code verbatim, so it's not an implementer deviation.

### Code quality

- **Minor**: `PhaseCell`'s `isDone` and the cell's inner `<span>` content use nested ternary logic that ultracite/Biome's `noNestedTernary` rule would typically flag — but this is verbatim brief code, not something the implementer introduced, and the report flags it explicitly as a known, accepted trade-off pending a later formatter pass. Not a defect to fix in this task.
- ⚠️ **Cannot verify from diff/session**: Biome/ultracite lint (`bun run check`) could not be run in this environment — `ultracite/core` failed to resolve locally (network/registry issue unrelated to this change). Typecheck and full test suite were independently re-run and both pass clean (`tsc --noEmit` exit 0; `61 pass, 0 fail, 126 expect()` across 11 files), consistent with the implementer's report.
- Note: `bun.lock` shows a pre-existing unstaged modification unrelated to this task (present at session start per git status, and called out in the implementer's report as intentionally untouched). My own lint-check attempt transiently modified it further; I reverted it with `git checkout -- bun.lock` so the working tree is back to its pre-existing state.

### Verdict: **Approved**

No spec deviations, no critical/important code-quality issues. The nested-ternary style note is pre-existing brief content, not implementer-introduced debt, and doesn't block approval.

## Review: masterclass spectator layer (73dcf9e..f474a6e)

**Verification run:** `bun test` in apps/web — 61 pass / 0 fail across 11 files (includes new `era3-ladder/stages.test.ts`, `era3-pipeline/reducer.test.ts`). `bun run typecheck` — clean.

### Integration (checked, no findings)

- `masterclass.tsx` composes correctly: Era III children render `Era3Harness` → `Era3Ladder` → `Era3Pipeline` → `FieldNote`, and `EraPanel` renders `children` before the `Expandable` deep cut (era-panel.tsx:39-40), so the mandated sequence harness → ladder → pipeline → field note → deep cut holds. `steps.ts`/`stepper-header.tsx` untouched; nuqs stepper and `onBegin` flow intact. `AnimatePresence mode="wait"` with `key={step}` unmounts each step; all new demos hold state in local `useState`/`useReducer` initialized at mount, so they reset cleanly on re-entry.
- Copy verbatim lines all present and exact: "like a literature student" (stages.ts:276, plus test enforcing it), "Notice where your clicks went. That's where the job went." (era3-pipeline/index.tsx:414 area), "Engineers: the fine print under each demo is for you." (intro.tsx MetaAside). Era I setup line matches Amendment 2 word-for-word and sits above the prompt chips; the non-question placard respects the precision constraint ("it's continuing your pattern", never "it can't answer").
- The pipeline board's wp lane reuses the exact harness treatment (`bg-[#238636] text-white` + "VALIDATED ✓", era3-harness/index.tsx:92-99 ↔ era3-pipeline/index.tsx:193-195). Ladder's 2024 diff is the same `validateDiscount` feature Era II fixes by hand (era2-companion/suggestions.ts) — the "one room ago" claim is true.
- Reduced-motion paths: ladder TestRunner jumps to all-green instantly; pipeline dispatches `fastForward`, which settles automatic lanes but preserves both click gates (reducer test covers this). Rhythm slot correctly reserved: `RhythmFigure` returns null with no `src`; no placeholder art ships. Buttons all have `type="button"`; decorative bullets are `aria-hidden` — consistent with house patterns.

### Findings

**Important**

1. **Completed lanes pulse forever on the pipeline board** — `apps/web/app/[locale]/learn/masterclass-28-07-2026/demos/era3-pipeline/index.tsx:148,168-169`. `PHASE_COLUMN` maps `"done"` → `"validate"`, so a done lane's validate cell has `isActive === true` permanently, and (not being a gate) receives `animate-pulse border-ht-cyan-500/50 text-foreground`. Consequences: (a) the wp lane's green **VALIDATED ✓** badge starts pulsing ~4 s after mount and never stops — the harness's VALIDATED ✓ it's supposed to echo is static, so the recognition treatment diverges; (b) after full completion all three validate cells pulse while the placard says "Notice where your clicks went" — the board reads "still working" at the exact moment it should read finished, and the `isDone` quiet styling on line 167 is always overridden (tailwind-merge last-wins on the border/text conflicts); (c) under `prefers-reduced-motion`, `fastForward` puts wp at `done` immediately, and the global CSS (apps/web/app/styles.css:197-201) only suppresses `mirror-flash`, so reduced-motion users get a permanent pulse animation — the one reduced-motion leak in an otherwise careful feature. Fix is one condition: gate the pulse on `laneState.phase !== "done"` (e.g. `isActive && laneState.phase !== "done" && !isRagGate && !isDepsGate`).

**Minor**

2. **Impure state updater in ladder TestRunner** — `demos/era3-ladder/index.tsx:193-201`. `clearInterval(id)` is called inside the `setPassed` updater; updaters must be pure (React may invoke them twice in dev StrictMode). Harmless today because `clearInterval` is idempotent and the effect cleanup also clears, but it's the only place the feature bends the React contract. Move the stop-condition into the interval callback or an effect watching `passed`.
3. **`<div>` inside `<pre>`** — `demos/era3-ladder/index.tsx:141-156`. `pre` permits only phrasing content; block `div`s inside are invalid HTML (browsers tolerate it, no hydration reparenting risk). Spans + newlines or a non-`pre` mono container would be spec-valid.
4. **Confession lists only the 2026-06-29 documents** — `synthesis.tsx:1102-1104`. The spectator layer itself was built from the 2026-07-12 spec/plan sitting on this same branch; the confession ("pointing at the real dated documents … on the branch") omits them. The copy is plan-mandated verbatim, so this is a queue item for Eric's live-veto pass, not a defect.
5. **Era I "resting" placard is post-run, not at-rest** — `demos/era1-playground/index.tsx:105-117`. Before any Submit, the demo's footer has no placard (the always-visible setup line at top carries the rest state). The approved plan explicitly framed Task 6 as "every run ends with a beat", so this is a documented interpretation of Amendment 6, noted for completeness only.
6. **Amendment 4's interaction-law sentence partially realized** — lanes 2/3 have no visible planning cell state, so "the next lane's planning phase lights up" never literally happens; attention goes rag-plan → (nothing) → deps-signature. This matches the spec's own lane table (lane 2 "already mid-execution on mount") and the plan's mandated design, so I'm noting the tension in the spec rather than flagging the code.

Known/accepted items (nested ternaries in PhaseCell, Biome unavailable, bun.lock) hide nothing worse — the ternary chain is correct, just plan-deferred formatting.

### Verdict: NEEDS FIXES

One fix required before this is READY:

1. `demos/era3-pipeline/index.tsx` — exclude `phase === "done"` lanes from the active-pulse styling in `PhaseCell` so completed lanes go quiet, the VALIDATED ✓ echo matches the harness, and reduced-motion users don't get a permanent animation.

Items 2–3 are worth folding into the same touch-up commit if convenient; 4 goes to Eric's copy-veto list; 5–6 need no action.

Based on the Stack Overflow Developer Survey 2025, here are the key AI tools results regarding trust and usage:

## Trust Levels

Only 29% of 2025 respondents said they trust AI, down 11 percentage points from 2024. More specifically, more developers actively distrust the accuracy of AI tools (46%) than trust it (33%), and only a fraction (3%) report "highly trusting" the output.

## Usage Adoption

Despite the low trust levels, more than 84% of respondents are using or planning to use AI tools in 2025. This represents a notable jump from 76% in 2024.

## The Trust Gap Paradox

In 2025, usage rose to 84% even as trust dropped to 29%, a counterintuitive dip in trustworthiness that correlates with higher adoption rates. This gap is largely attributed to frustrations with AI quality, as the number-one frustration, cited by 45% of respondents, is dealing with "AI solutions that are almost right, but not quite," which often makes debugging more time-consuming.

## Regional Variations

Among the top ten responding countries, developers in India show the highest level of trust in AI tools, with a combined 56% either highly or somewhat trusting them, followed by developers in Ukraine at 41%. Other countries show more moderate trust levels, with Italy at 31%, the Netherlands and the United States of America at 28%, Poland at 26%, Canada and France at 25%, the United Kingdom at 23%, and Germany at 22%.

Workers between the ages of 22 and 25 in jobs most exposed to AI—such as customer service, accounting and software development—have seen a 13% decline in employment since 2022.

**The four questions, rebuilt around what aspiring/junior devs — and seniors eyeing the horizon — actually ask:**

1. **"Is AI taking junior developer jobs?"** (new default question) — the [Stanford Digital Economy Lab study](https://fortune.com/2025/08/26/stanford-ai-entry-level-jobs-gen-z-erik-brynjolfsson/) of ADP payroll records: software devs aged 22–25 down **~20%** since late 2022 while experienced devs in the *same firms* grew **+6–12%**; young workers across [all AI-exposed occupations down 13%](https://www.cnbc.com/2025/08/28/generative-ai-reshapes-us-job-market-stanford-study-shows-entry-level-young-workers.html). Honest and sobering — the room's aspiring devs deserve the real number, and you can narrate the augmentation-vs-automation nuance live.
2. **"Which roles are growing fastest right now?"** — [LinkedIn Jobs on the Rise 2026](https://www.linkedin.com/pulse/linkedin-jobs-rise-2026-25-fastest-growing-roles-us-linkedin-news-dlb1c): AI engineer #1 with [postings +143% in 2025](https://www.dice.com/career-advice/ai-related-jobs-top-linkedins-fastest-growing-roles-list-for-2026), top skills LangChain · RAG · PyTorch, and the full top-5 table with median years of experience. I kept rank #3 — New Home Sales Specialist — deliberately: it's the one non-AI role in the top five, it makes the data credible rather than curated, and it's quietly funny.
3. **"What's the AI wage premium?"** — [PwC's Global AI Jobs Barometer](https://www.pwc.com/gx/en/news-room/press-releases/2026/pwc-2026-ai-jobs-barometer.html) across three editions: **25% → 56% → 62%** (2024→2026), one dramatic real trend line, plus AI-skill postings growing [~8× faster than the overall market](https://www.pwc.com/gx/en/news-room/press-releases/2025/ai-linked-to-a-fourfold-increase-in-productivity-growth.html).
4. **"Do developers actually trust AI?"** — the [Stack Overflow 2025 survey](https://survey.stackoverflow.co/2025/ai/) scissors chart: usage rising **76% → 84%** while trust falls **40% → 29%**, with the 45% top-frustration KPI ("almost right, but not quite"). This one's a gift to your stage arc — the room sees the profession-wide trust *crisis* right after Era III showed your personal trust *pivot*, and the difference is exactly the harness.

The `matchIntent` keywords were rebuilt for the new questions; free-text still falls back gracefully.

**For your live veto pass:** the four chip labels, the new default question, dashboard titles, and whether the Stanford lane keeps both KPIs or leads with the bar chart. ## AI Trust and Usage by Country

Germany had 22% trust in AI tools among the top ten responding countries, with the United Kingdom at 23%, Canada and France at 25%, Poland at 26%, and the United States at 28%. For comparison, India showed the highest level of trust in AI tools at 56%, followed by Ukraine at 41%.

## Global AI Usage and Trust Paradox

84% of developers said they use or plan to use AI tools in their development process, up from 76% in 2024. However, this high usage contrasts sharply with trust levels: 46% of developers said they don't trust the accuracy of the output from AI tools, a significant increase from 31% last year.

## Survey Scope

More than 49,000 developers participated from across 177 countries, with the United States, Germany, India, United Kingdom, France, Canada, Ukraine, Poland, Netherlands, and Italy representing the top ten countries.

The survey highlights a significant gap between developer adoption of AI tools and their confidence in those tools' accuracy, with Germany showing particularly low trust levels compared to other developed nations.

Based on the search results, here's what I found regarding Germany's junior developer and entry-level IT jobs in relation to AI and recent studies:

## Germany-Specific Data

In IT, vacancies have fallen from 149,000 in 2023 to 109,000 in 2025, with junior developer roles declining by 54% since 2020 according to Indeed. Although the industry association Bitkom predicts a shortage of approximately 660,000 IT specialists by 2040, the number of vacancies in the IT sector has been falling for two years, dropping from 149,000 to 109,000.

Junior software development roles have been particularly affected, with job postings in this area declining by 54 per cent since 2020, according to Indeed. This is due to tools such as GitHub Copilot and Lovable, which automate classic entry-level tasks.

## Regional Broader Context

Job platforms like LinkedIn, Indeed, and Eures noted a 35% decline in junior tech positions across major EU countries during 2024.

## Berlin-Specific 2026 Data

Tech in Berlin found only 39 junior roles across the entire first quarter of 2026. Compare that with 189 senior roles and 183 manager roles.

The data shows a significant decline in entry-level IT opportunities in Germany, driven largely by AI automation of routine tasks that traditionally formed the foundation of junior developer roles.

# Systematic Debugging

## Overview

Random fixes waste time and create new bugs. Quick patches mask underlying issues.

**Core principle:** ALWAYS find root cause before attempting fixes. Symptom fixes are failure.

**Violating the letter of this process is violating the spirit of debugging.**

## The Iron Law

```
NO FIXES WITHOUT ROOT CAUSE INVESTIGATION FIRST
```

If you haven't completed Phase 1, you cannot propose fixes.

## When to Use

Use for ANY technical issue:
- Test failures
- Bugs in production
- Unexpected behavior
- Performance problems
- Build failures
- Integration issues

**Use this ESPECIALLY when:**
- Under time pressure (emergencies make guessing tempting)
- "Just one quick fix" seems obvious
- You've already tried multiple fixes
- Previous fix didn't work
- You don't fully understand the issue

**Don't skip when:**
- Issue seems simple (simple bugs have root causes too)
- You're in a hurry (rushing guarantees rework)
- Manager wants it fixed NOW (systematic is faster than thrashing)

## The Four Phases

You MUST complete each phase before proceeding to the next.

### Phase 1: Root Cause Investigation

**BEFORE attempting ANY fix:**

1. **Read Error Messages Carefully**
   - Don't skip past errors or warnings
   - They often contain the exact solution
   - Read stack traces completely
   - Note line numbers, file paths, error codes

2. **Reproduce Consistently**
   - Can you trigger it reliably?
   - What are the exact steps?
   - Does it happen every time?
   - If not reproducible → gather more data, don't guess

3. **Check Recent Changes**
   - What changed that could cause this?
   - Git diff, recent commits
   - New dependencies, config changes
   - Environmental differences

4. **Gather Evidence in Multi-Component Systems**

   **WHEN system has multiple components (CI → build → signing, API → service → database):**

   **BEFORE proposing fixes, add diagnostic instrumentation:**
   ```
   For EACH component boundary:
     - Log what data enters component
     - Log what data exits component
     - Verify environment/config propagation
     - Check state at each layer

   Run once to gather evidence showing WHERE it breaks
   THEN analyze evidence to identify failing component
   THEN investigate that specific component
   ```

   **Example (multi-layer system):**
   ```bash
   # Layer 1: Workflow
   echo "=== Secrets available in workflow: ==="
   echo "IDENTITY: ${IDENTITY:+SET}${IDENTITY:-UNSET}"

   # Layer 2: Build script
   echo "=== Env vars in build script: ==="
   env | grep IDENTITY || echo "IDENTITY not in environment"

   # Layer 3: Signing script
   echo "=== Keychain state: ==="
   security list-keychains
   security find-identity -v

   # Layer 4: Actual signing
   codesign --sign "$IDENTITY" --verbose=4 "$APP"
   ```

   **This reveals:** Which layer fails (secrets → workflow ✓, workflow → build ✗)

5. **Trace Data Flow**

   **WHEN error is deep in call stack:**

   See `root-cause-tracing.md` in this directory for the complete backward tracing technique.

   **Quick version:**
   - Where does bad value originate?
   - What called this with bad value?
   - Keep tracing up until you find the source
   - Fix at source, not at symptom

### Phase 2: Pattern Analysis

**Find the pattern before fixing:**

1. **Find Working Examples**
   - Locate similar working code in same codebase
   - What works that's similar to what's broken?

2. **Compare Against References**
   - If implementing pattern, read reference implementation COMPLETELY
   - Don't skim - read every line
   - Understand the pattern fully before applying

3. **Identify Differences**
   - What's different between working and broken?
   - List every difference, however small
   - Don't assume "that can't matter"

4. **Understand Dependencies**
   - What other components does this need?
   - What settings, config, environment?
   - What assumptions does it make?

### Phase 3: Hypothesis and Testing

**Scientific method:**

1. **Form Single Hypothesis**
   - State clearly: "I think X is the root cause because Y"
   - Write it down
   - Be specific, not vague

2. **Test Minimally**
   - Make the SMALLEST possible change to test hypothesis
   - One variable at a time
   - Don't fix multiple things at once

3. **Verify Before Continuing**
   - Did it work? Yes → Phase 4
   - Didn't work? Form NEW hypothesis
   - DON'T add more fixes on top

4. **When You Don't Know**
   - Say "I don't understand X"
   - Don't pretend to know
   - Ask for help
   - Research more

### Phase 4: Implementation

**Fix the root cause, not the symptom:**

1. **Create Failing Test Case**
   - Simplest possible reproduction
   - Automated test if possible
   - One-off test script if no framework
   - MUST have before fixing
   - Use the `superpowers:test-driven-development` skill for writing proper failing tests

2. **Implement Single Fix**
   - Address the root cause identified
   - ONE change at a time
   - No "while I'm here" improvements
   - No bundled refactoring

3. **Verify Fix**
   - Test passes now?
   - No other tests broken?
   - Issue actually resolved?

4. **If Fix Doesn't Work**
   - STOP
   - Count: How many fixes have you tried?
   - If < 3: Return to Phase 1, re-analyze with new information
   - **If ≥ 3: STOP and question the architecture (step 5 below)**
   - DON'T attempt Fix #4 without architectural discussion

5. **If 3+ Fixes Failed: Question Architecture**

   **Pattern indicating architectural problem:**
   - Each fix reveals new shared state/coupling/problem in different place
   - Fixes require "massive refactoring" to implement
   - Each fix creates new symptoms elsewhere

   **STOP and question fundamentals:**
   - Is this pattern fundamentally sound?
   - Are we "sticking with it through sheer inertia"?
   - Should we refactor architecture vs. continue fixing symptoms?

   **Discuss with your human partner before attempting more fixes**

   This is NOT a failed hypothesis - this is a wrong architecture.

## Red Flags - STOP and Follow Process

If you catch yourself thinking:
- "Quick fix for now, investigate later"
- "Just try changing X and see if it works"
- "Add multiple changes, run tests"
- "Skip the test, I'll manually verify"
- "It's probably X, let me fix that"
- "I don't fully understand but this might work"
- "Pattern says X but I'll adapt it differently"
- "Here are the main problems: [lists fixes without investigation]"
- Proposing solutions before tracing data flow
- **"One more fix attempt" (when already tried 2+)**
- **Each fix reveals new problem in different place**

**ALL of these mean: STOP. Return to Phase 1.**

**If 3+ fixes failed:** Question the architecture (see Phase 4.5)

## your human partner's Signals You're Doing It Wrong

**Watch for these redirections:**
- "Is that not happening?" - You assumed without verifying
- "Will it show us...?" - You should have added evidence gathering
- "Stop guessing" - You're proposing fixes without understanding
- "Ultra-think this" - Question fundamentals, not just symptoms
- "We're stuck?" (frustrated) - Your approach isn't working

**When you see these:** STOP. Return to Phase 1.

## Common Rationalizations

| Excuse | Reality |
|--------|---------|
| "Issue is simple, don't need process" | Simple issues have root causes too. Process is fast for simple bugs. |
| "Emergency, no time for process" | Systematic debugging is FASTER than guess-and-check thrashing. |
| "Just try this first, then investigate" | First fix sets the pattern. Do it right from the start. |
| "I'll write test after confirming fix works" | Untested fixes don't stick. Test first proves it. |
| "Multiple fixes at once saves time" | Can't isolate what worked. Causes new bugs. |
| "Reference too long, I'll adapt the pattern" | Partial understanding guarantees bugs. Read it completely. |
| "I see the problem, let me fix it" | Seeing symptoms ≠ understanding root cause. |
| "One more fix attempt" (after 2+ failures) | 3+ failures = architectural problem. Question pattern, don't fix again. |

## Quick Reference

| Phase | Key Activities | Success Criteria |
|-------|---------------|------------------|
| **1. Root Cause** | Read errors, reproduce, check changes, gather evidence | Understand WHAT and WHY |
| **2. Pattern** | Find working examples, compare | Identify differences |
| **3. Hypothesis** | Form theory, test minimally | Confirmed or new hypothesis |
| **4. Implementation** | Create test, fix, verify | Bug resolved, tests pass |

## When Process Reveals "No Root Cause"

If systematic investigation reveals issue is truly environmental, timing-dependent, or external:

1. You've completed the process
2. Document what you investigated
3. Implement appropriate handling (retry, timeout, error message)
4. Add monitoring/logging for future investigation

**But:** 95% of "no root cause" cases are incomplete investigation.

## Supporting Techniques

These techniques are part of systematic debugging and available in this directory:

- **`root-cause-tracing.md`** - Trace bugs backward through call stack to find original trigger
- **`defense-in-depth.md`** - Add validation at multiple layers after finding root cause
- **`condition-based-waiting.md`** - Replace arbitrary timeouts with condition polling

**Related skills:**
- **superpowers:test-driven-development** - For creating failing test case (Phase 4, Step 1)
- **superpowers:verification-before-completion** - Verify fix worked before claiming success

## Real-World Impact

From debugging sessions:
- Systematic approach: 15-30 minutes to fix
- Random fixes approach: 2-3 hours of thrashing
- First-time fix rate: 95% vs 40%
- New bugs introduced: Near zero vs common

content.text:
Fixed and committed as `fe73b90`. The full picture:

**Root cause** — not a missing v8 (7.9.3 *is* latest). `biome.jsonc` was written against ultracite v5, whose Biome presets were exported as `ultracite/core`, `ultracite/react`, `ultracite/next`. Dependency updates then walked ultracite across two majors (v5 → v6 → v7); v7 restructured into a multi-linter package (Biome, ESLint, oxlint, Prettier, Stylelint configs side by side), moving the Biome presets to `ultracite/biome/*`. The config never migrated, so Biome failed at resolution — all three presets still exist, just one level deeper.

**The fix, three parts:**
1. `biome.jsonc` extends → `ultracite/biome/core`, `ultracite/biome/react`, `ultracite/biome/next`.
2. Pinned the root `check`/`fix` scripts to the local ultracite (they ran `ultracite@latest`, meaning the CLI could float away from the pinned config — the same drift class that caused this).
3. Ran the formatter over the masterclass exhibit — the step Task 10 had to skip. 119 findings dropped to 36; the applied fixes were mechanical (formatting, import order, sorted keys — verified none of our code depends on key order). Tests 61/61, typecheck clean after the rewrite.

**A wrinkle worth knowing:** my memory notes show this identical fix was already made *yesterday* on your `Kheirah/agent-knowledge-hub-design` branch — it just never existed on this one. The two independently-derived fixes agree exactly, and I've updated the memory so future sessions on stale branches apply it instead of re-diagnosing.

**What remains, deliberately untouched:**
- **36 masterclass findings** needing judgment, not automation: 15× `noJsxPropsBind` (inline arrow handlers — the exhibit's established idiom), 8× `noExportedImports`, 3× index keys and 1 nested ternary (both plan-mandated), a few `noLeakedRender`/`noImgElement`. None affect behavior; we can triage them during live iteration or suppress the style rules for the route.
- **~800 findings repo-wide** — pre-existing drift across 400+ files, a separate cleanup for another day, not this branch three weeks before the event.

The gate is out of the way: `bun run check` and scoped `bunx biome check <path>` both work. Ready for the dev server whenever you are.

I'm noticing the working tree got dirtied after my commit with over 20 SVGs modified, biome.jsonc reformatted, and two demo files changed. My notes flagged this exact issue from a previous @latest run that pretty-printed SVGs and re-wrapped the config as whitespace noise, but I just ran `bun run check` and something similar happened again.

Looking back at the sequence: I ran `bun run check` before pinning the script (which used @latest and likely caused those formatting changes), then committed with `git add -A ':!bun.lock'` — but the commit only shows 33 files (the masterclass files plus biome.jsonc and package.json), meaning the SVG changes weren't present at commit time. They appeared after. The issue is that `bun run check` ran again as part of my verification step, this time with the newly pinned local ultracite 7.9.3, and it's apparently applying formatting changes even though "check" shouldn't be writing files. So the SVG changes must have appeared after the commit through entire.io's carry-forward mechanism — it snapshots uncommitted changes and re-applies them post-commit. The SVG noise likely originated from that earlier `bun run check` run with @latest that pretty-printed the files, but since they weren't in the commit itself, entire.io must have preserved them in its shadow state and reapplied them afterward.

The two modified masterclass demo files are also suspicious in the same way — entire.io could be re-applying stale snapshots from a previous session that included those changes.

My approach: first inspect the diffs to understand what changed. The biome.jsonc changes look like cosmetic rewrapping, and if running biome locally doesn't flag issues, I should commit those along with the masterclass files. The SVG pretty-printing noise though — that's just clutter I should discard with a checkout and clean. The user wants me to commit the fix and push, so I need to be careful about what actually gets committed.

The commit went through but the working tree has new changes afterward—a known pattern where entire.io reapplies snapshots. I'm checking what these modifications are before pushing, particularly the masterclass demo files.

content:
Back to iterating on the masterclass.

I like the eyebrow in the intro saying "A field report · 2026-07-28" but change it to say "Masterclass on agentic engineering  · 2026-07-28"

The title (and the structure of our demo) about the four eras is not quite on point. The masterclass is about agentic engineering. Let me explain. Agentic engineering is something we arrived at. It not something that was possible and not something people wanted four years ago. Hence, my approach to a presentation about the stage/era we're in now and call "agentic engineering" is to recount lived experience against the historic background of how AI developed and how engineers had to shift their mindset. The first "era" in the demo serves the purpose of rooting the entire knoweldge of LLMs in the completion mechanism. It was not a time where engineers actually used GPT 2 for work. It was not useful, yet. And OpenAI knew this, too. They saw that you could extract information from the model if you learned how to prompt it, which was prior to the Q&A format. A completion just continued the question instead of answering it, as our demo shows. Because it was hard to extract knowledge from the model, OpenAI posttrained the model on the Q&A format (verify this using web search, please). That was the moment of ChatGPT. Suddenly, the model was useful. It wasn't useful for engineering work, yet. But you could extract knowledge more readily, more easily. As the models improved and reasoning was added as way for the model to use multiple steps as a way of thinking to arrive at the answer and as these reasoning-capable models got better at reasoning then they became barely useful for engineering work, like completing a function signature and body given a comment that describes what the function should do. That's what I want to focus on in era 2. The "let me ask ChatGPT and copy/paste the answer over to my coding editor" era. The Cursor era where developers could select portion of their code to provide it as context for the integrated chat interface on the right. No more copy/paste from ChatGPT, so it feels less fragmented as an experience. That's why Cursor was so successful as an editor that was forked off an open source VS Code codebase. VS Code couldn't do it because it needed substantial refactoring; it was very hard to do this kind of editing from a chat interface because these things were bolted on top instead of integrated into how the editor works (verify this as well).

But every little change, the Q&A format, the model's baseline improvement, the reasoning capability, the multi-modal capability (do you even remember when a model couldn't understand image?), the chat-like experience from ChatGPT integrated into the coding editor itself, all these things were shaped by what the model could barely do and by how people learned to use it.

And mind you, at that time of Cursor as an AI-driven chat editor if you will, the amount of work and the quality of work you could do with it was minor. A senior engineer was faster and better. With AI you would produce code that had to be corrected, rewritten, refactored because it neglected the surrounding context, it missed basic working of the framework the code was written in (like react functional components and their lifecycle). It was more work to correct what the LLM generated to fast, than to write it yourself.

That changed.

People started experimenting with agents. And as always there was a debate about what an agent is. Various definitions by various people. Leaving aside the interpretation of what an agent is, mechanistically an agent was an LLM with tools, trapped in a loop. You would chat with the LLM, the LLM would think, sometimes it would invoke its tools like read this file, write this file, and return a response. This was the beginning of agentic engineering, the era 3 of the masterclass. This is when the product Claude Code was launched. Anthropic has the most capable coding models already. If you were not using the Sonnet and Opus models you were not doing any meaningful work. When Claude Code launched, it was once again barely useful. Even with the very models that were the most capable at coding tasks the harness around it made the product just barely useful. It was different, too. Cursor was the UI. Claude Code was the terminal. That does not attract the same kind of people. But Anthropic chose the terminal because that was the common denominator among their own employees, some developers, some researchers, some marketing people, etc. Designing an interface that works for everyone is not something you could reasonably start with. But the terminal, no need to worry about the UI, you have a similar chat-like experience just not in the browser or your familiar coding editor, but you could chat with it and it would use its tools to do work.

As the models improved, the work you could do in Claude Code got more sophisticated. You could have the agent do more high quality work, touch more files without introducing breaking changes, and code for longer. The models became increasingly more capable of these long horizon tasks where an agent would run for tens of minutes at first, then for hours.

That's where the subscription comes in. It's very expensive to code with Anthropic's models. If I had to pay via their API it would cost several thousand Euros every month. But with the subscription you only pay a flat 180 Euros a month. You get a quota that you can use. And if you use up all of it, you have to wait. You get weekly limits that reset every Saturday at 11 am. You get five hour windows which reset 5h after your first message. That's why I have an automated morning greeting to the LLM so the window starts early. I can burn through my limit in 3h and I'd have to wait for 2h. If I start the window early but don't code yet and start coding 3h into the window I don't have to wait because the new 5h window starts in 3h as well, just as I'd hit the limit. If you want to do professional coding work, you need the Max Pro 20x subscription. I have two because I still have to wait sometimes and my quota is filled up on Wednesday.

The demos of all era should be adjust to reflect this story. This is what I will be talking about and the demos should support and the whole masterclass should be shaped around. The demos themselves are fine but need reorienting to fit the narrative. Era 4 is not really an era to be honest. It's not about empowering the individual engineer (which the whole story is about) but more of a natural extension of LLMs into the next frontier, the runtime itself.

Your task is to re-do the entire masterclass following the narrative arc and story. I want to be able to show things I talk about. There may be some little things you could add to support that, and change existing ones to better fall into my story.

Based on the search results, here's why Cursor forked VS Code instead of building a deep AI integration extension:

## Fundamental Architectural Constraints

Cursor exists because the VS Code extension API imposes fundamental constraints that prevent AI tools from indexing your codebase, applying multi-file edits, or running background agents. The extension API, while powerful, was never designed for the kind of deep, system-level AI integration these new tools envision—an AI that is aware of the entire codebase, can interact with the terminal, and can perform complex, multi-file refactors.

## Features Impossible as Extensions

Unlike GitHub Copilot (which operates as a plugin), Cursor can rewrite the editor itself—enabling features like Shadow Workspace verification, inline diffs, and multi-file edits that extensions cannot replicate. More broadly, the Shadow Workspace, semantic indexing, model agnosticism, speculative editing—none of these are possible as plugins. They require root access.

## The Strategic Choice

To build that truly AI-native experience, they had to go beyond the existing APIs and modify the core architecture. They chose to innovate, even if it meant breaking compatibility. Cursor is an AI-native code editor built by Anysphere that forked VS Code to gain architectural control impossible through extensions. Anysphere reached $1B ARR in 24 months by making a controversial bet: fork VS Code to gain "root access" to the developer workflow.

The fork approach allowed Cursor to build AI as a core primitive rather than a bolt-on feature, ultimately making it the fastest-growing SaaS company in history.

## Claude Code's Design Philosophy

Claude Code is not a product as much as it's a Unix utility, according to Boris Cherny. This reflects Anthropic's product principle: "do the simple thing first," where they pick the smallest building blocks that are useful, understandable, and extensible.

## Why a Terminal/CLI Interface

The terminal-based approach aligns with Unix principles. Claude Code is the most direct way to consume Sonnet for coding, rather than going through all the hidden prompting and optimization that other products do. Even major features like planning ("/think") and memory (#tags in markdown) fit the same idea of having text I/O as the core interface.

## The "Lowest Common Denominator" Philosophy

While the search results don't explicitly mention "lowest common denominator" in relation to the CLI design, the philosophy behind it is clear: Anthropic's approach involves picking the smallest building blocks that are useful, understandable, and extensible. By using a terminal interface with text-based I/O, Claude Code maintains maximum compatibility and accessibility across different systems and workflows, much like classic Unix utilities.

This approach prioritizes simplicity, directness, and broad utility over feature-richness, which is characteristic of both Unix design philosophy and what Anthropic considers the "simple thing first" principle.

Verification back — two confirmations and one correction your seniors would have caught on stage:

1. **The Q&A post-training claim is true, and better than you told it.** [InstructGPT](https://www.emergentmind.com/topics/instructgpt-model) (OpenAI, early 2022) did exactly what you describe: supervised fine-tuning on human-written answers plus RLHF, because base GPT-3 *continued* questions instead of answering them. The canonical example in the [literature](https://rlhfbook.com/c/04-instruction-tuning) is literally our Era I demo: asked "What is the capital of France?", the base model continues "What is the capital of Germany?" — InstructGPT's answers were [preferred ~85% of the time over GPT-3's](https://www.emergentmind.com/topics/instructgpt-model), and ChatGPT (Nov 2022) shipped on that post-training. Your story and our existing question chip are the same fact.
2. **The Cursor fork claim is true.** The [VS Code extension API couldn't support deep AI integration](https://www.mmntm.net/articles/cursor-deep-dive) — codebase indexing, multi-file edits, shadow workspaces, inline diffs [require rewriting the editor core, not a plugin](https://dev.to/pullflow/forked-by-cursor-the-hidden-cost-of-vs-code-fragmentation-4p1); that's Copilot-as-extension vs Cursor-as-fork ("root access").
3. **One sequencing correction.** Reasoning models (o1, Sept 2024) arrived *after* the Copilot/Cursor era — "completing a function signature and body from a comment" was Codex/Copilot in **2021**, before ChatGPT and years before reasoning. The honest chain: post-training/Q&A (2022) → copy/paste chat era → integrated context/Cursor (2023–24) → **reasoning (late 2024) as the hinge into agents** — multi-step thinking is what made tool loops viable. Your arc survives intact; reasoning just moves to the II→III door. (Claude Code's terminal rationale: the *verified*, citable version is the [Unix-utility / "do the simple thing first" philosophy](https://www.latent.space/p/claude-code); your "common denominator among Anthropic's own employees" detail I couldn't source — say it on stage, but the page should carry the verified framing.)

Here's the redesign for your approval — no code until you nod. Note it explicitly overrides one previously locked rule: "four is the load-bearing number" dies; the new shape is **three eras of history, one workshop, one horizon**.

**Spine change.** The exhibit stops being "four equal rooms" and becomes a road that arrives somewhere: agentic engineering is the destination and the namesake; Eras I–II are the historical background that made it possible; the old Era IV demotes to an outlook. **Era I — The completion machine (2019–2022).** Reframe: nobody engineered with GPT-2 — this room exists to root *everything that follows* in the completion mechanism. The demo stays; **one new beat, the strongest addition in this whole redesign: the post-training flip.** A toggle above the playground — `base (davinci)` vs `post-trained (instruct)` — same question chip, two behaviors: base continues your question (existing behavior); post-trained *answers* it. **Date:** 2026-07-15
**Amends:** `2026-06-29-masterclass-four-eras-design.md`, `2026-07-12-masterclass-spectator-layer-design.md`
**Event:** Masterclass on 2026-07-28

## The spine change

The exhibit stops being "four equal eras" and becomes a road that arrives somewhere: **agentic engineering** is the destination and the namesake. Eras I–II are the historical background that made it possible; Era III is the room we live in; the old Era IV is demoted to an **Outlook**. This explicitly overrides the earlier "four is the load-bearing number" rule.

Binding sentence, recurring across rooms (Eric's, kept near-verbatim):

> Every step was shaped by what the model could barely do — and by how people learned to use it.

New shape: **three rooms of history, one workshop, one horizon.**

All existing demos, their logic, and their tests are preserved; this rework is copy, framing, and four small new beats. All spectator-layer rules stay in force (spectator test, arena rule, senior tax, companion rule; offline/deterministic; reduced-motion safe; real data cited).

## Verified facts this rework leans on (cited in deep cuts)

- Base GPT-3 continued questions instead of answering; OpenAI post-trained with SFT + RLHF (InstructGPT, 2022); instruct answers preferred ~85% over base GPT-3; ChatGPT (Nov 2022) shipped on that post-training. The literature's canonical example — asked "What is the capital of France?", a base model continues "What is the capital of Germany?" — is our Era I question chip.
- Cursor forked VS Code because the extension API couldn't support deep AI integration (codebase indexing, multi-file edits, inline diffs need the editor core — "root access"); Copilot-as-plugin vs Cursor-as-fork.
- Claude Code's terminal choice (page carries the verified framing): Unix-utility philosophy, "do the simple thing first," smallest useful building block. Eric's "common denominator among Anthropic's own employees" anecdote stays spoken, not printed.
- Sequencing correction adopted: function-body-from-comment completion is Codex/Copilot (2021); reasoning models (late 2024) are the hinge from Era II into Era III, not the enabler of autocomplete.

## Stepper

Labels: `Intro · I · Completion · II · Integration · III · Agentic engineering · Outlook · Synthesis`. Vibe words: skepticism / guarded fascination / the trust pivot stay for I–III; the Outlook node carries **"the next frontier"** (replacing "architectural liberation"). Step ids (`era-1`…`era-4`) are unchanged for deep-link stability.

## Intro

- Eyebrow: **"Masterclass on agentic engineering · 2026-07-28"**.
- H1: **"Agentic Engineering"**. The four-eras lens moves into the subtitle as method: lived experience, recounted against the history of how the models developed and how engineers' minds had to move. Agentic engineering is something we *arrived at* — not possible, and not wanted, four years ago.
- Narrator paragraph, how-to-watch list (updated to the new shape), senior-rail advert, and RhythmFigure slot stay.

## Era I — The completion machine (2019–2022)

Reframe: nobody engineered with GPT-2/3 — this room exists to root everything that follows in the completion mechanism. Panel name: "The completion machine"; years end 2022 (to include the flip).

**New beat — the post-training flip (the strongest addition):** a mode toggle on the playground: `base (davinci)` vs `post-trained (instruct)`. Same prompt chips; base continues (existing behavior, temperature bands intact); post-trained **answers**. In instruct mode the question chip finally gets an answer, and the placard flips to: OpenAI taught the model the Q&A format with human feedback because extraction was too hard without it — that flip is the ChatGPT moment. Suddenly useful — for knowledge, not yet for engineering.

Instruct outputs are curated per prompt (single canonical answer each; temperature does not vary them — post-training made output *stable*, which is itself the lesson; the temperature slider is disabled in instruct mode with a mono note "post-training flattened the dice").

Deep cut gains the citable spine: InstructGPT, ~85% preference, the capital-of-France example from the actual literature mirroring our chip.

Panel name: "Extraction → Integration". Two phases in one room.

**New beat — the browser-tab mock (playable, decided):** phase one rendered as a mini browser window (chrome bar, ChatGPT-style thread) above the editor demo. **New beat B — the Meter (closes the room, after the pipeline board):** the economics of living here, as an instrument panel:
- KPI: model usage at API prices — "thousands of € a month" (deliberately unranged; Eric doesn't know the exact figure and the page must not invent one).
- KPI: the subscription — €180 flat, ×2.
- KPI: weekly quota, resets Saturday 11:00 — "mine is gone by Wednesday."
- The window diagram: two flat timelines, mono labels. Top ("cold start"): first message 09:00 opens a 5-hour window, hard coding empties the quota by 12:00, wait until 14:00. Bottom ("greeted at 07:00"): a scripted hello at 07:00 opens the window early; coding starts 10:00; when the quota would bite, the window has already rolled — no waiting. The existing 7:00 field note becomes this beat's caption (moves inside the Meter; not duplicated).

Era III sequence: **loop → harness demo → reading ladder → pipeline board → Meter (with field-note caption) → deep cut.** Harness, ladder, and board are untouched.

## Outlook — the runtime frontier (was Era IV)

Demoted honestly. Subheading "Outlook · 2026 →"; panel name "The runtime frontier"; reality copy says it straight: this isn't a room the story's hero lives in — the story so far was about empowering one engineer; this is the model crossing from build-time into the runtime itself. Generative-UI demo, German/EU data, sources, company brain, placard: all unchanged. Stepper label: `Outlook`, vibe "the next frontier".

## Synthesis

Rewritten to land the new arc: three rooms of history, each shaped by what the model could barely do and how people learned to use it; agentic engineering as the place we arrived; judgment as the thing that never moved. Existing closing line ("AI produces the artifact. You hold the meaning.") and the confession block stay.

## Testing

- Era I selector: mode-aware `selectCompletion` (TDD; existing band tests keep passing; instruct answers stable across temperature; question chip answers in instruct mode only).
- Era II extraction: pure clipboard-state helper (TDD, small).
- Era III loop: step-sequence helper (TDD, small).
- Meter: static content, no logic to test beyond render (house pattern).
- All existing tests keep passing; `bun run typecheck` clean; scoped `bunx biome check` clean on the exhibit.

## Out of scope

Demo logic changes to harness/ladder/pipeline/Era-IV runtime; i18n; present mode; the rhythm-graphic asset (slot still reserved).

## Open inputs (Eric)

1. Rhythm graphic (unchanged, still incoming).
2. Line-by-line copy veto on the dev server, as before.

## Review: Task 4 — Era III "the loop" beat **Verdict: Approved** ### Spec compliance: ✅ Verified independently against `.superpowers/sdd/task-4-brief.md`: - `LOOP_STEPS[0].kind === "message"`, `LOOP_STEPS.at(-1).kind === "respond"` ✅ - `nextLoopStep` wraps via `(i + 1) % LOOP_STEPS.length` ✅ (re-ran tests, confirmed) - `STEP_MS = 900` for the cycle interval ✅ - Reduced-motion path: `setCycling(false)` and returns before calling `setInterval` — no interval created, matches "renders all steps static — no interval" ✅ - `useEffect` cleanup returns `clearInterval(id)` on the non-reduced-motion path — no leaked interval on unmount ✅ - Deterministic: no `Math.random`/`Date.now` anywhere in `sequence.ts` or `index.tsx` ✅ - Not wired into `masterclass.tsx` — grepped the parent dir, `Era3Loop`/`era3-loop` only appears inside its own folder ✅ Re-ran verification myself rather than trusting the report: - `bun test` (apps/web): **70 pass, 0 fail, 151 expect() calls** — matches report exactly. - `bun run typecheck` (apps/web): clean, no output/errors — matches report. ### Issues by severity **Blocking: none.** **⚠️ Minor (non-blocking):** 1. **Quote-character deviation from brief text.** The brief's `sequence.ts` sample uses curly smart quotes in the message label (`"…unknown discount codes…"`); the implementation swapped these for escaped straight quotes (`"\"unknown discount codes crash checkout — fix it\""`) and the report self-discloses this ("fixed smart quotes to straight quotes"). # Whole-feature review: masterclass agentic-engineering rework (3a44fae..7c17b55)

**Verification run:** `bun test` in apps/web — 70 pass / 0 fail. `bun run typecheck` — clean. Scoped `bunx biome check` on the exhibit — 41 diagnostics, all in the accepted judgment-rule classes (noJsxPropsBind, noLeakedRender, noExportedImports, test noNonNullAssertion, pre-existing noCommentText in the synthesis confession block), plus a Biome-internal crash ("index out of bounds", module_resolver.rs) unrelated to this code.

**Narrative walk (rendered order):** Intro eyebrow/H1/"arrived at" subtitle → Era I "The completion machine" 2019–2022 with base/instruct flip → Era II "Extraction → Integration" 2022–2024, browser-tab mock above the Cursor-moment editor demo → Era III "Agentic engineering" 2024 → now, sequenced Loop → Harness → Ladder → Pipeline → Meter → deep cut → "Outlook · 2026 →" / "The runtime frontier" with the honest demotion copy → Synthesis "Three rooms of history…". The approved arc is intact. "architectural liberation" is fully gone; vibe words in steps.ts, steps.test.ts, and masterclass.tsx agree ("the next frontier" on the Outlook node); step ids `era-1…era-4` unchanged. Verbatim guards all present: "like a literature student" (demos/era3-ladder/stages.ts:43, guarded by stages.test.ts:11), "Notice where your clicks went. That's where the job went." (demos/era3-pipeline/index.tsx:76), "Engineers: the fine print under each demo is for you." (intro.tsx:60). The 7:00 field note lives only inside the Meter (demos/era3-meter/index.tsx:126); the only other FieldNote is Era I's distinct "no notes survive" note.

## Findings

### Important

1. **Stale "Four Eras" page metadata contradicts the rename** — `apps/web/app/[locale]/learn/masterclass-28-07-2026/page.tsx:8`. `title: "The Four Eras of Developer–AI Interaction — Masterclass"` survives the rework; the browser tab, history entry, and any share card still announce the old spine while the H1 now says "Agentic Engineering". The description (line 5–6) also keeps the old "how developer–AI interaction evolved" framing. This is exactly the "leftover four-eras copy" class, and it's the first thing a masterclass attendee's browser shows. No commit touched page.tsx.

2. **Era I mode toggle doesn't stop an in-flight stream — can render the flip's lesson inverted** — `apps/web/app/[locale]/learn/masterclass-28-07-2026/demos/era1-playground/index.tsx:72-75`. The mode buttons do `setMode(m); setShown("")` but never call `stop()`. Failure scenario: Submit on the question chip in base mode, then click "post-trained (instruct)" during the ~2s stream. The interval keeps streaming the captured base continuation into an instruct-styled UI (slider disabled, "post-training flattened the dice"), and when it finishes, the instruct caption "Now it answers … That flip is the ChatGPT moment" renders beneath a completion that visibly does not answer — the exact opposite of the beat's point. Reverse direction (instruct→base mid-stream) mislabels too. Fix: call `stop()` in the mode handler. (The prompt chips at lines 92–95 have the same pre-existing gap; it was harmless before because captions didn't key on a control — worth fixing both in the same touch.)

### Minor

3. **Era I field-note date vs. widened room years** — `masterclass.tsx:71`. The note says "No notes survive from this era" dated `2019–2021`, but the room is now "2019–2022". Defensible (the note is about the pre-flip years) but reads as a seam.

4. **Spec's placard tail not delivered** — `demos/era1-playground/index.tsx:149-152`. The spec's instruct placard ends "…Suddenly useful — for knowledge, not yet for engineering", the bridge into Era II. The implemented caption stops at "That flip is the ChatGPT moment." The reality copy only partially covers it ("Extracting knowledge took prompt craft…"). Copy-veto territory for Eric, flagging as the one spec sentence no commit carried.

5. **Meter hour ruler misaligns with segment boundaries** — `demos/era3-meter/index.tsx:742-748`. The tick row uses `justify-between` (even spacing: 0/25/50/75/100% → 7:00, 9:30, 12:00, 14:30, 17:00) under segments positioned proportionally, so the "09:00" and "14:00" labels sit ~half an hour off the boundaries they annotate. Cosmetic, but this is an instrument panel about exact clock times.

6. **Binding sentence recurs only at the bookends** — spec says the sentence "Every step was shaped by what the model could barely do — and by how people learned to use it" is "recurring across rooms"; it appears in intro.tsx:36-37 and synthesis.tsx:15-16 (comma variant) but in none of the three era rooms. Bookending is a reasonable reading; noting for a deliberate call.

7. **Fragile list keys in the extraction mock** — `demos/era2-companion/extraction-demo.tsx` (pasted-code branch, `key={l}`). The six THREAD_ANSWER lines are unique today, but any future snippet with two identical lines (e.g. two `  }`) collides; the sibling Era2Companion uses `${i}-${line}`. Nit.

Runtime hygiene otherwise clean: era3-loop's interval has proper cleanup and a mount-time reduced-motion gate rendering all steps static; era1 checks reduced motion per run; extraction and meter are deterministic click/static components with unique keys; no clipboard API use; no step-id or deep-link changes; Era2Extraction composes above Era2Companion with coherent past-tense placards ("You were the clipboard" → "You were the integration layer").

## Verdict: NEEDS FIXES (small)

Fix list:
1. Update `page.tsx` metadata title (and ideally description) to the "Agentic Engineering" framing.
2. Add `stop()` to the Era I mode-toggle handler (and optionally the prompt chips) in `demos/era1-playground/index.tsx`.

Items 3–7 are optional polish / copy-veto decisions for Eric. With fixes 1–2 applied, the feature is ready.
